name: The Traders Oak

location.address: Traders Oak Park, Samuels Avenue, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Traders Oak Park, north of downtown

access: Free. In Traders Oak Park, a small city park named after the tree.
story:
Fort Worth's first lasting business opened under this oak, because the army would not let it any closer. When Camp Worth went up in 1849 on the bluffs where the West and Clear forks of the Trinity River meet, federal rules kept merchants at least a mile from the post. So Henry Clay Daggett and Archibald Franklin Leonard built a log trading post at a safe distance, among a stand of sprawling live oaks near Cold Springs.

It worked. Soldiers, settlers and Native Americans came to trade and to rest at the springs, and the store became the first successful business in Fort Worth. In 1850 the first election in what is now Tarrant County was held in front of it, and the voters chose Birdville as county seat. The county's first court sat inside. When the army abandoned the fort in 1853, the two traders moved their business up to an empty building on the bluffs.

The tree stayed where it was. The city's heritage register calls it perhaps the best-known tree in Fort Worth, says it has grown here for well over 200 years, and has it marking the spot where the trading post stood. What the register does not give is the species. The cabin went up among live oaks, but nobody has written down that this is one of them, so we list it simply as an oak. If you know which, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old oak the little park is named after, marking where the 1849 trading post stood. It stands in Traders Oak Park, off Samuels Avenue.

name: Van Zandt Cottage Live Oak

location.address: Beside the Van Zandt Cottage, Trinity Park, Fort Worth, TX

access: Free. In Trinity Park, public park ground.
story:
This live oak keeps watch over the oldest building in Fort Worth still standing where it was built: the Van Zandt Cottage. The house belonged to Major Khleber Van Zandt, one of the most influential men in the city's early history, and the land around it was his too. His home and acreage took in ground that is now Trinity Park, the Fort Worth Botanic Garden and the Cultural District, so this whole corner of town, museums and gardens included, is one man's former property divided up.

The oak is the cottage's companion rather than its subject. The city's heritage register records it as a large live oak beside the house and says nothing about when it took root, so we cannot tell you whether the major sat under it, planted it or never gave it a thought. Nobody has dated it and nobody has published its girth. If you know either, tell us.

A second listed live oak grows about 80 metres to the east, in the small parking area off Farmhouse Way, so the two make an easy pair. The Botanic Garden, with its own champion trees, is a short walk south.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large live oak right beside the Van Zandt Cottage. It stands in Trinity Park; the other listed oak, about 80 metres east, is the one in the parking area off Farmhouse Way.

name: Van Zandt Farm Live Oak

location.address: Small parking area off Farmhouse Way, east of the Van Zandt Cottage, Trinity Park, Fort Worth, TX

access: Free. In Trinity Park, public park ground.
story:
For years this live oak was hidden behind a shed. A ramshackle storage building along Crestline Road blocked it from view; today the tree is the centrepiece of a small parking area off Farmhouse Way. It is an odd kind of promotion, from overlooked to the thing everyone parks around, but it means you can now see the whole of it.

It grows in Trinity Park, just east of the Van Zandt Cottage, on ground that belonged to Major Khleber Van Zandt, whose home and acreage once took in this park, the Botanic Garden next door and the Cultural District. The city's heritage register singles the tree out as a fine specimen. It gives no age and no measurements, so how big the trunk is remains for you to judge on the spot. If you bring a tape measure, tell us what you find, and if you know when it was planted, tell us that too.

Its neighbour at the cottage, the other listed live oak, is about 80 metres west, so both take five minutes.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the live oak in the middle of the small parking area off Farmhouse Way. It stands in Trinity Park, about 80 metres east of the Van Zandt Cottage.

name: Steele's Tavern Oak

location.address: Site of Steele's Inn and Tavern, north side of downtown Fort Worth, TX

story:
Fort Worth's official mail arrived, from 1856, at the spot where this live oak grows. Steele's Inn and Tavern stood here, it handled the town's official mail service, and it was the end of the line for the stagecoach between Fort Worth and Jacksboro.

That made it a waystation on a very long road. Passengers from the southern and eastern states stopped at the inn to rest before riding on to Jacksboro, where they could join the Butterfield Overland Stage, the route that carried them across the Southwest and on into California.

The inn is long gone and the oak remains, which is why the city's heritage register lists it. What the register does not say is how old the tree is, or whether it was already standing when the coaches pulled up. It would be easy to claim it watched them; nobody has shown that it did. If you know when it was planted, or have measured its trunk, tell us.

The Pioneers Rest ash is about a kilometre away and the Traders Oak another kilometre beyond it, so the three make a single morning's walk on the north side of downtown.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the live oak on the site of the old Steele's Inn and Tavern. It stands on the north side of downtown, about a kilometre southwest of Pioneers Rest Cemetery.

name: Royal Flying Corps Live Oak

location.address: Commonwealth War Graves plot, Greenwood Memorial Park, Fort Worth, TX

access: Free. In Greenwood Memorial Park cemetery (the city register calls it Greenwood Cemetery), open to visitors in daylight.
story:
A live oak in a Fort Worth cemetery shades the graves of First World War airmen from the Royal Flying Corps. It stands over a group of Commonwealth War Graves in Greenwood Memorial Park, the resting place of pilots killed in training exercises in Tarrant County during the war.

They were trained fast and for dangerous work: taking aerial photographs of German positions and shooting down observation balloons, on as little as fifteen hours in biplanes. More than 1,500 pilots earned their wings in Fort Worth. The men under this tree died here, in training, thousands of kilometres from the war they were preparing for.

The same cemetery holds the Turner Oak, the oldest dated tree in the city, about 300 metres away by the main entrance. This one has no plaque about buried gold and no recorded age; the city's heritage register lists it for what it stands over rather than for its size, and gives no measurements. We also have no recent sighting of it beyond that register. If you visit, tell us it is still there and roughly how big it is.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the live oak standing over the small group of Commonwealth War Graves. It stands in Greenwood Memorial Park, about 300 metres northeast of the Turner Oak at the entrance.

name: Inspiration Point Live Oak

location.address: Inspiration Point, Marion Sansom Park, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Marion Sansom Park, above Lake Worth

access: Free. In Marion Sansom Park, public park ground.
story:
Fort Worth's official register of heritage trees lists this live oak partly for the view and partly, with a straight face, for the stolen kisses it has watched. It grows at Inspiration Point in Marion Sansom Park and has looked out over Lake Worth, the register says, for generations.

Beside it stands an old rock shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Depression-era work programme. Tree and shelter together are the reason to come: a wide view over the lake and the country around it, and a piece of the park's past within arm's reach.

What nobody has written down is the tree's age. "For generations" is the register's phrase, and we will not sharpen it into a number. Nor does the register give a girth or a height, or say whether the oak was already here when the shelter went up. If you have measured it, or know more about either of them, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the old rock shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps right beside it. It stands at Inspiration Point in Marion Sansom Park, looking out over Lake Worth.

name: George T. Reynolds Live Oak

location.address: Arrow S Park, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Arrow S Park, west Fort Worth

access: Free. In Arrow S Park, public park ground.
story:
This old live oak in Arrow S Park grows on what was once part of George T. Reynolds' ranch, and that ranch is where a whole string of places around it came from. Reynolds was one of the founders of the Reynolds Cattle Company, a name known on the range from Texas all the way up to Canada. Over time he gave away or sold parts of his land, and those pieces became Mosque Point, once called Reynolds Point, Camp Leroy Shuman, Amon Carter's Shady Oak Farm, Arrow S Park itself and more.

So the tree belongs to an expansive cattle ranch that turned, parcel by parcel, into ground other people could use. The city's heritage register calls it a great, old tree and leaves it at that: no age, no girth, no planting date. Whether it was already shading cattle when Reynolds owned the land is a reasonable guess and still only a guess. If you know more about it, or have put a tape round the trunk, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the great old live oak the city lists in Arrow S Park. It stands on land that was once part of George T. Reynolds' cattle ranch.

name: The TCU Original Oak

location.address: Texas Christian University campus, just west of University Drive and northeast of Reed Hall, Fort Worth, TX

access: Free, on the open Texas Christian University campus.
story:
When Texas Christian University moved onto its permanent Fort Worth campus, it had exactly one tree, and the students had to bring it themselves. A small plaque in the turf, dedicated in 2011, says so: the only tree on the new campus was this live oak, transplanted "from the forest" by the class of 1912.

That class had reason to care. Fire had destroyed the university's former home in Waco, and they were the first students to graduate from the new grounds in Fort Worth. In the spring of 1912 they worked with the Texas Shade Tree Company to dig up a large live oak growing in woods near the campus and move it onto the site. This one took.

Everything else grew up around it. The campus is now thick with trees, and this is where they started. The Original Oak spreads its canopy across the middle of the grounds, just west of University Drive and northeast of Reed Hall.

Nobody has recorded its age. It was already a large tree when the seniors moved it in 1912, so it is well over a century old, and how much older is anyone's guess until somebody measures it. If you know its girth, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small 2011 plaque in the turf beside it, reading Original Oak Tree. It stands in the middle of the TCU campus, just west of University Drive and northeast of Reed Hall.

name: National Champion Chittamwood

location.address: By the Fort Worth Botanic Garden and Trinity Park, Fort Worth, TX

access: Near the Fort Worth Botanic Garden and Trinity Park. The register does not say whether the tree stands inside the garden, which charges admission, or on free park ground.
story:
No chittamwood in the United States is bigger than this one. The city's heritage register records it as the largest of its kind in the country, a national champion of Sideroxylon lanuginosum, a tree that also goes by the name gum bumelia.

That is the whole of the record, and it is enough for a detour. The register gives no girth, no height and no age, so we cannot tell you how big the biggest one actually is, only that nobody has put a larger one on the books. If you have measured it, tell us.

It grows on the edge of the Botanic Garden and Trinity Park. The register does not say whether its spot falls inside the garden's paid grounds or on free park land, and we would like to know that too. Either way it sits in good company: the two Van Zandt live oaks are about 700 metres north, the Botanic Garden's record jujube about 500 metres west, and the Will Rogers mesquite, another national champion, a little over a kilometre away.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the chittamwood, also called gum bumelia, the largest of its kind in the United States. It stands near where the Fort Worth Botanic Garden meets Trinity Park.

name: The Hollow Pecan

location.address: Rock Springs area, Fort Worth Botanic Garden, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Fort Worth Botanic Garden (Rock Springs section), Cultural District

access: Paid entry. Inside the Fort Worth Botanic Garden, in the Rock Springs area; the garden charges general admission and keeps set opening hours.
story:
By the city's own estimate this pecan is more than 200 years old, and Fort Worth's heritage register counts its visitors in layers. Native Americans came first. Then traders, before there were settlers to trade with. Then the pioneering families who built the town, and after them the tens of thousands who have walked through the Botanic Garden since.

It grows in the Rock Springs area of the garden, where the jujube that holds the Texas record for its species stands a couple of hundred metres away, so one ticket covers two listed trees.

The name is the register's, and it does not explain it, so we will not describe a hollow we have not seen. What the register does give is the estimate, and it is an honest one: over 200 years, with no upper figure and no measurement behind it that we know of. If you have taped the trunk, or know where the estimate came from, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big old pecan in the Rock Springs area of the Botanic Garden. It stands about 200 metres south of the garden's champion jujube.

name: Quanah Parker Park Pecan

location.address: Quanah Parker Park, Fort Worth, TX
location.neighbourhood: Quanah Parker Park, east Fort Worth

access: Free. In Quanah Parker Park, public park ground.
story:
Size is why this pecan made Fort Worth's heritage register. It stands more than 85 feet tall, about 26 metres, and its trunk is more than 160 inches round, which is over four metres. The register gives its age as 150 years or more and singles out its shape as well.

Put those numbers beside the Turner Oak, the city's oldest dated tree, and the pecan holds its own: a trunk of roughly the same girth, on a tree about twice as tall. Where the oak spreads, the pecan climbs.

That is the whole of the record. It grows in Quanah Parker Park on the east side of the city, a long way from the other trees on this page, and the register says nothing about who planted it or what it has stood through, so neither will we. A tree that size is easy enough to find once you are in the park. If you know its story, or when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, more than 26 metres tall with a trunk over four metres round. It stands in Quanah Parker Park, on the east side of Fort Worth.

name: Timberline Post Oak
age_estimate: "likely one of the oldest trees in Fort Worth" (register; no figure)

location.address: Behind a stop sign at an intersection, southeast Fort Worth, TX

access: Visible from the public street: it stands directly behind a stop sign at an intersection. Stay on the pavement and do not cross private gardens.
story:
Road crews have come for this corner more than once, and every time the post oak has been left standing. Fort Worth's heritage register says the tree has been spared by roadwork on numerous occasions, and the proof is where it stands: directly behind a stop sign at a busy intersection, the kind of spot where trees usually lose.

The register also calls it ancient, likely one of the oldest trees in the whole city. It gives no figure, and we will not supply one. Without a core, a planting date or even a recorded girth, "one of the oldest" is as far as the evidence goes, and it is a strong enough claim from a city that also holds the Turner Oak.

We have no recent sighting of it beyond the register itself. If you pass it, tell us it is still there and how big it is, and if you know its age, tell us that too.

You see it from the street, which is the right way to see it: stay on the pavement and leave the gardens around it alone.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the post oak growing directly behind the stop sign at a busy intersection. Look from the pavement; it stands in southeast Fort Worth.

name: Memorial Bur Oak

location.address: Southwest Fort Worth, TX (setting not stated by the register)

access: Access not stated by the register: check whether the point is public ground before publishing.
story:
This bur oak used to be the biggest of its kind in Texas. It has since lost the state title, but Fort Worth's heritage register says it remains the second largest bur oak in the state, which is a great deal of tree to find in the southwest of the city.

That ranking is close to everything on record. The register gives no girth, no height and no age, and it says nothing about what the tree is a memorial to, despite the name it carries. Somebody chose that word for a reason. If you know whose memory it keeps, or have ever measured the trunk, tell us.

What we can vouch for is shorter but useful. The pin is the city's own point for this tree, not a street address, and a naturalist logged a bur oak at that spot within the last four years, so it was standing recently.

In autumn, look down. Bur oaks drop the largest acorns of any North American oak, sitting in deep cups with a mossy fringe, and a tree this size should leave plenty of them.

One thing to check before you set out: the register does not say whether the ground around the tree is public, so look at the spot on the map first and do not go through any gate that is not open to you.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the massive bur oak the city lists as the second largest in Texas and a former state champion. It stands at the register's point in southwest Fort Worth.
not_merged_reason: Held 2026-10-20: access unknown (hard rule 10). Nominatim puts the point about 75 m from the Trinity Trails Fort Worth Branch path by the Clear Fork, town Benbrook, but says nothing about the ground at the pin; Overpass timed out. Publish once a source or map shows the point is on public ground.

name: Forest Park Witness Tree
age_estimate: standing in 1845, so roughly two centuries or more
access: Free. In Forest Park, public park ground.
story:
In 1845 a surveyor chose this bur oak to mark the land, and it is still here to be found. The E.S. Harris survey of that year used it as a witness tree: a living survey point, often fixed to establish a corner, so the line could be found again. Surveyors picked such trees for staying power, durable and slow to rot. Bur oak was a favourite, because it lives long and stands up to fire.

The reasoning held. The oak had a partner, a second witness tree from the same survey, which stood beside it until 2014, when it was removed after drought and the stresses that came with it. This one is still in Forest Park, more than 180 years after it went into the record.

That is also the floor for its age. It was standing in 1845, so it is at least 180 years old, and a tree chosen as a durable landmark was presumably no sapling even then. Nobody has put a firmer number on it. If you know its girth, tell us, and the range can get a top end.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the bur oak that served as a survey marker in 1845; its partner from the same survey was removed in 2014. It stands in Forest Park.

name: John Peter Smith Oak

location.address: Darnell Street parking lot and lawn, east of the Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth, TX

official_register.name: City of Fort Worth Heritage Trees (designated 24 April 2009)

access: Stands at the centre of the Kimbell Art Foundation's Darnell Street lot and lawn east of the museum; the museum's student-tour page says groups may eat under it, the lawn is designed for visitor recreation. Hours not published; not checked.
transport: Beside the Kimbell Art Museum, Cultural District; transit not checked.
story:
In 1982 Fort Worth's school district called this oak likely the oldest living thing in the whole district, and named it after the man who founded the city's public schools. Today it belongs to an art museum, which laid out its new grounds around it.

The land has changed hands more often than the tree. The city's heritage register says it once belonged to the pioneer Major Khleber Van Zandt, whose cottage still stands with its own listed live oak about 600 metres away in Trinity Park. It was donated to the city, became a school site and then held the district's administration building. At the district's centennial the oak was named for John Peter Smith, founder of the public school system and, in the register's words, the father of Fort Worth. The city listed it as a heritage tree in 2009.

The Kimbell Art Museum now owns and cares for it. The oak is the centrepiece of the museum's new lawn east of the building, designed for the tree's long-term health, and school groups on tours may eat lunch under it.

It is a low, wide tree: 4.5 metres round and 13.7 metres tall, with a crown about 28 metres across, twice its height, and the thickest live oak on this page. The museum calls it centuries old, but no source puts a number on it, and the newest dated report we found is from 2018. If you have seen it lately, or know its age, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 28 metres across on a tree under 14 metres tall. It stands in the middle of the lawn and parking lot on Darnell Street, east of the Kimbell Art Museum.

name: The Botanic Garden Southern Magnolia

location.address: Fort Worth Botanic Garden, Old Garden Road near Rock Springs Road, 3220 Botanic Garden Blvd, Fort Worth, TX 76107

official_register.name: City of Fort Worth Heritage Tree Program (Heritage Trees map layer), no. Heritage layer OBJECTID 27 (DFW Co-Champion Southern Magnolia)

access: Paid entry. Fort Worth Botanic Garden is city-owned and open to visitors in garden hours (a ticketing page lists 8 am to 5 pm daily, last entry 4 pm; sources disagree on summer hours and on which areas the ticket covers). Free parking in the main lots.
transport: Inside the Fort Worth Botanic Garden, Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth; Trinity Metro bus routes serve the Cultural District, no rail.

name: The Heritage Courtyard Live Oak

location.address: Fort Worth Museum of Science and History, Heritage Courtyard, 1600 Gendy Street, Fort Worth, TX 76107

official_register.name: City of Fort Worth Heritage Tree Program (Heritage Trees map layer), no. Heritage layer OBJECTID 6 (Ruth Carter Stevenson Live Oak)

access: Paid entry. The oak stands in the museum's enclosed Heritage Courtyard; museum open Tuesday to Saturday 10 am to 5 pm, Sunday noon to 5 pm, closed Monday (fwmuseum.org). No source gives a separate courtyard charge or hours; it appears to be inside general admission. Confirm the courtyard is open on the day.
transport: Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth, next to the Will Rogers Memorial Center and Amon Carter Museum; Trinity Metro bus routes serve the district, no rail.

location_site.name: Heritage Courtyard, Fort Worth Museum of Science and History

verify_notes: Flagged: city register plus one encyclopedia line. City Heritage Tree layer (OBJECTID 6, owner of the programme): in the early 1950s Ruth Carter Stevenson, daughter of Amon Carter and driving force behind the Amon Carter Museum, planted trees along Burnett-Tandy Drive 'because she loved to plant trees' and 'because the space was so empty'; they adorned the museum when it opened in 1954; most were cleared when a major expansion began in 2007 but one was spared, now the feature of the enclosed courtyard, with the architect blending the building to it; the layer says Bartlett Tree Experts donated time and resources to keep it alive (Bartlett claim from the city layer only, not confirmed elsewhere). Wikipedia on the museum independently says the museum kept one tree from the original courtyard and built around it, in an open area called the Heritage Courtyard (the museum's own event page also places the Oak Room beside the courtyard). Age basis: documented planting 'early 1950s' for the trees of this planting, the city layer says the spared tree is one of them; stays broad, about 65 to 80 years (derived from the city's planting date). Date conflict: one source says the museum opened 1945 as a children's museum; the layer says the building opened 1954. Alive: iNaturalist observation 2023-12-11 within the pin (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/193722638, lifecheck RECENT); no later dated check found. Pin: city coordinate 32.74392,-97.36940 is inside the museum footprint (OSM museum relation bbox 32.7435-32.7450, -97.3698 to -97.3686); the site is one small courtyard, approximate. 360westmagazine.com returned a bot block (fast fail). No girth or height found. Recognise: the one large oak in the museum's enclosed courtyard (city layer wording).
story:
When Fort Worth's Museum of Science and History was rebuilt from 2007, one live oak was allowed to stay, and the new building was shaped around it. It now stands on its own in the museum's enclosed Heritage Courtyard.

It got there in the early 1950s. Ruth Carter Stevenson, daughter of Amon Carter and the driving force behind the Amon Carter Museum, planted trees along Burnett-Tandy Drive, by the city's account because she loved to plant trees and because the space was so empty. They were there to frame the museum when its building opened in 1954. The museum's own beginnings are dated differently elsewhere, to 1945 as a children's museum, so take 1954 as the building's date, not the institution's.

The 2007 expansion cleared most of Stevenson's trees. This one was spared. The city's heritage register says the architect blended the building to the tree, and credits Bartlett Tree Experts with giving time and resources to keep it alive; that last part we have only from the city.

Counted from her planting, it is about 65 to 80 years old. Nobody has published its girth or height, and they hardly matter here. What makes the tree is that somebody decided a museum should bend for it.

The courtyard is inside the museum, which charges admission and is closed on Mondays, so check it is open on the day.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one large oak in the museum's enclosed Heritage Courtyard, the only tree kept from the 1950s planting when the building went up around it.

name: The Harley Live Oaks

location.address: Trail Drive at the Fort Worth Botanic Garden edge, between the Botanic Garden and the Will Rogers Memorial Center, Fort Worth, TX 76107

official_register.name: City of Fort Worth Heritage Tree Program (Heritage Trees map layer), no. Heritage layer OBJECTID 8 (Harley Live Oaks)

access: Free. Trees at the edge of Trail Drive on City of Fort Worth parkland (Botanic Garden grounds, realigned parkland), viewable from the public road and sidewalk; no source states the exact legal status of the strip, OSM shows Trail Drive as a public tertiary road at the point.
transport: Cultural District, about 4.5 km west of downtown Fort Worth; about 300 m from Trinity Park's Van Zandt trees (ftw_007, ftw_008); Trinity Metro bus routes serve the district, no rail.

City Heritage Tree layer (OBJECTID 8): a cluster of live oaks saved when Harley Avenue (now Trail Drive) was realigned; trees were slated for removal, saved by the City Forester, a State Forester and other municipal departments and by realigning parkland at the Botanic Garden; they now form 'a green gateway into the Will Rogers Exhibition area'. The City Urban Forestry Council slideshow 'Heritage Trees of Fort Worth' (ctufc.org PDF) was fetched but not read (no pdftotext on the runner); a search extract says it also lists 'Harley Street Live Oaks' saved from a similar fate, not verified from the file itself. No count, girth, height or age found; saved-from-removal date not given (Harley Ave realignment era unknown). Ensemble: a stand with one place to stand at the roadside; if the writer cannot name which trunk is biggest, treat as a stand, not a single tree. Pin approximate, a stand coordinate.
story:
A road was moved to keep these live oaks. When Harley Avenue was realigned into what is now Trail Drive, the trees were slated to come out. The City Forester, a State Forester and several other city departments stepped in, and the answer was to rework the parkland at the edge of the Botanic Garden so the road could pass and the oaks could stay.

They now line the way into the Will Rogers exhibition grounds, which the city's heritage register calls a green gateway. It is a fair description of what a cluster of live oaks does to the start of a road.

The register is our only written source, and it is short on numbers. It does not say how many trees there are, how big any of them is, how old they are, or even when the road was moved. We have not picked out one trunk as the champion, so treat this as a stand you take in from the roadside rather than a single tree. If you know when Harley Avenue became Trail Drive, or have counted or measured the oaks, tell us.

What we can say is that a naturalist logged an observation at the spot in October 2026, and that they make an easy stop on a longer walk. Trinity Park's Van Zandt live oaks are about 300 metres away.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the cluster of live oaks lining the edge of Trail Drive at the Botanic Garden. They stand beside the road on the way into the Will Rogers exhibition grounds, visible from the sidewalk.
